title: The Spread of Information Disorder on Facebook and its Impact on Sociocultural Sustainability
evidence: Table 2 'Mechanisms for the spread of information disorder': Sharing 13 (26%), Amplification 12 (24%), Influential user pages 10 (20%), algorithmic recommendations 8 (16%), echo chambers 5 (10%), filter bubbles 2 (4%), TOTAL 50 (100%)
reason: no qualifying share: the only quantitative result is a 100%-summing breakdown of which spreading MECHANISM each of the 50 informants named; no share of respondents who encountered information disorder is reported (denominator-sets-construct rule gives a share of mechanisms not of exposed people)
notes: REVERSAL of abstract ELIGIBLE. Full text shows the questionnaire arm covered only 25 of the 50 informants (25 did interviews) and its only tabulated output is the mechanism breakdown. Exposure findings are reported purely qualitatively ('many young adults frequently encounter Facebook pages rife with misinformation'; 'information disorder is pervasive') with no number. Table 1 is demographics only.

title: The Quality of Dermatology Match Information on Social Media Platforms: Cross-Sectional Analysis
denominator: 21 sources discussing away rotations (of 34 total sources)
evidence: 'Twenty-one articles covered the topic of away rotations, of which 19 (90.5%) recommended doing an away rotation... whereas 8 (38.0%) articles said to complete as many away rotations as possible, in contrast to the official APD letter which recommends completing no more than 2 away rotations'
reason: advice that CONTRADICTS a published standard is accuracy and counts (coverage-is-not-accuracy rule read in the positive direction)
notes: No whole-corpus (n=34) inaccuracy share is reported; every share has a topic-conditional denominator. Other shares: 10/15 (66.7%) of sources on grades stressed AOA status vs 39.7% of matched residents actually AOA (comparison to a base rate, not a truth judgement per se); 16/22 (72.7%) recommended a research year vs 6/22 (27.3%) against (disagreement, no standard contradicted); 3/6 vs 3/6 on broad vs focused interests. HUMAN CHECK: abstract says 15 Reddit posts, manuscript says 14 (34 = 10 TikTok + 14 Reddit + 10 SDN); '11 of these (52.3%)' should be 52.4%; several denominators below 20. Table 1 is a means comparison (Step scores, publication counts), not a share.

title: Digital Natives, Critical Strangers: The Challenge of Student Critical Literacy in Indonesia's Post-Truth Era
denominator: 8 interviewed students
evidence: 'Sebagian besar responden dalam penelitian ini mengakui bahwa mereka pernah mempercayai hoaks, dengan proporsi sebesar 75%, sementara hanya 25% yang menyatakan tidak pernah' (English: 'Most respondents in this study admitted they had believed a hoax, at a proportion of 75%, while only 25% said they never had'); Table 5 lists 6 of 8 respondents as 'Pernah Percaya Hoaks = Ya'
reason: self-reported past encounter with a hoax; being deceived by one entails having met it
notes: BORDERLINE CONSTRUCT: the item measures having BELIEVED a hoax, not merely having seen one, so it is a self-reported deception rate rather than a pure exposure rate. Denominator is 8, far below the 20 floor the instructions flag. HUMAN CHECK: the paper is internally inconsistent. Two different tables are both numbered 'Tabel 5' (one with 6 respondents on epistemic authority, one with 8 on misinformation experience); respondent names differ across tables (Dinda/Raka/Nesa... in Table 2, Adinda/Bayu/Cindy... in Tables 3-4, Alifa/Rio/Nadine... in Table 5), so the 8 'participants' are not consistently the same 8 people; methods say 15-20 respondents were planned; the 75% figure also appears only in Gambar 2 (a figure) besides the sentence quoted. Non-English (Indonesian) source, translation given above.

title: The use of social media in the creation political awareness of youth in Delta State
denominator: 475 survey respondents (of 500 distributed)
evidence: Table 2 item 2 'Most political information on social media are false and unreliable': SA 177 (37%) + A 97 (20%); text: 'the respondents identified the peculiar nature of social media political awareness to be false, unreliable (N =58%; X = 3.4; SD =1.5)'
reason: perceived amount of falsity in what the respondent sees is self-reported recall (perceived exposure)
notes: Value is an agreement rate with a perception statement, not a direct 'how often did you encounter' item. 177+97=274/475=57.7%, so 58% is right and the rounded row percentages (37+20=57) are the source of the 1-point gap. HUMAN CHECK: text and table disagree elsewhere in Table 2 (text reports item 4 as 'N=52%; X=3.1; SD=1.6' while the table row shows 69+9=78% and X=4.1; text cites 'N=86%; X=1.9' for an item the table marks Reject), and Table 3 row 1 is garbled. Also available: 16.4% always / 55.4% very often exposed to social media generally (Table 1), which is exposure to the platform, not to misinformation.

title: The Effectiveness of Social Media in Customer Risk Awareness
denominator: 3,600 posts across six platforms over 12 months
evidence: 'Of the 3,600 posts analyzed...' and 'Misinformation cues, such as unverified claims and contradictory or debunked content, were observed for around one in 5 posts, but higher prevalence on short-form video platforms and lower prevalence on platforms with stronger moderation policies'; abstract: 'One fifth of the total sampled posts included deceptive markers'
reason: share of sampled posts coded as carrying misinformation
notes: FLAG FOR HUMAN BEFORE EXTRACTING. Three problems. (1) The code is mixed: 'unverified claims' is a verifiability/credibility marker, not a truth judgement, and is pooled with 'contradictory or debunked content' which is; no separate share for the accuracy component. (2) The value is only ever given as 'around one in 5' / 'one fifth' - no table, no exact count, no per-platform numbers despite platform differences being claimed, no reported kappa value ('exceeded the recommended level'). (3) The paper's prose is degraded to the point of suggesting machine generation ('The word out.'; 'more and 233 more customers'; 'sector-2 perception of risk severity tension between attention getting'), the author is an unaffiliated independent researcher, and the journal is a pay-to-publish AI/ML title. Other approximate shares: 'almost half' of posts from peers/influencers, 'over half' emotionally framed, 'only about a third' with actionable steps. The N~1200 experiment is a stimulus study, not prevalence.

title: INVESTIGATING THE ROLE OF SOCIAL MEDIA IN MEDIA LITERACY EDUCATION AMONG POST GRADUATION STUDENTS OF TUMKUR
denominator: 93 postgraduate students
evidence: 'Exposure to fake news or misleading content is common, with 48.39% of the respondents encountering it sometimes, 22.58% frequently, and 19.35% rarely. Only 9.68% students reported never encountering such content.'
reason: self-reported frequency of encountering fake news or misleading content
notes: 90.3% is the ever-encountered share, derived as 100 - 9.68 (never); the paper does not print it as a single figure, it prints the four-category frequency breakdown, which sums to exactly 100.00. Full breakdown for extraction: frequently 22.58%, sometimes 48.39%, rarely 19.35%, never 9.68%. Denominator 93 valid respondents. Verification-practice percentages (32.41% always verify etc.) are a skills measure and out of scope; the mean awareness ratings (2.6 fake news, 2.76 misinformation) are also out of scope.

title: A study exploring the relationship between social media use and nutrition-related practices among secondary school students in London
denominator: 24 London secondary school students aged 16-18+
evidence: 'Of the 24 participants (54% female)... Although 71% had encountered nutrition misinformation, few consistently verified the nutrition qualifications of creators (13%), and most didn't routinely fact-check (54%)'
reason: self-reported share who had encountered nutrition misinformation
notes: The 'full text' is a one-page Nutrition Society conference abstract (OCE1 E38) - there is no methods or results section beyond the paragraph quoted, so no item wording, no recall period and no confidence interval are recoverable. Denominator 24, just above the 20 the instructions flag; 71% of 24 = 17.0 participants. Other shares in the same paragraph are behaviour, not exposure (79% altered their diet, 71% purchased products, 71% influenced by brands/influencers). Fact-checking and verification percentages are a skills measure and out of scope.

title: Who Uses Right-Wing Alternative Online Media? An Exploration of Audience Characteristics
evidence: 'Only alternative news websites to which a right-wing bias could be attributed were included in the analysis. The bias attribution was based on previous studies' (Section 3.1); Table 2 lists the 21 sites (Unzensuriert, MV-Lehti, Junge Freiheit, RT Deutsch, Compact, PI-News, Nyheter Idag...)
reason: stance is not falsity: the site list is assembled by attributed RIGHT-WING BIAS, not by any unreliability, credibility or accuracy rating, so the usage share is a partisan-media reach figure with no truth judgement anywhere in the paper
notes: REVERSAL of the first-pass INCLUDE (which was never adjudicated). The number, if the review ever decides hyperpartisan-outlet lists are in scope: 931/8048 (11.6%) of Reuters DNR 2019 respondents in Austria, Germany, Sweden and Finland reported using at least one listed site for news in the past week; 355 (4.4%) used two or more. Two further caveats. (1) It is SELF-REPORTED survey recall of a site list, not log or panel data, so it could not be AUDIENCE EXPOSURE or REACH as those constructs are defined here. (2) The per-country usage values (7.91, 7.27, 8.66, 22.45%) and awareness values (24.15, 50.45, 19.58, 52.66%) exist only in Figure 1. Secondary analysis of Reuters DNR data - check overlap with any DNR-based study already in the corpus.

title: Comparing covariation among vaccine hesitancy and broader beliefs within Twitter and survey data
evidence: 'we could reliably infer a user's stance on particular beliefs based on assessing the stances of the websites they linked to... coded the stances of each tweet as agree (+1) or disagree (-1)'; the corpus is 8,064,173 tweets returned by 29 belief-specific search queries built from the survey's belief items
reason: two rules independently: stance is not falsity (tweets are coded agree/disagree with a belief, never true/false), and a misinformation-only corpus has no prevalence (the tweets were retrieved BY searching for the conspiracy and vaccine-hesitancy claims themselves, so no wider denominator exists)
notes: Confirms the abstract stage's UNSURE as an exclude, not a reversal. The paper's aim is methodological (does Twitter data reproduce the covariance structure of survey beliefs under PCA), not descriptive. Table 2's percentages are the distribution of how many belief tags each account or respondent carried (90.7% of Twitter accounts had one non-zero tag), not a prevalence of anything. Survey side (615 responses) measures belief endorsement, which is out of scope in any case.

title: How Do University Students' Web Search Behavior, Website Characteristics, and the Interaction of Both Influence Students' Critical Online Reasoning?
evidence: Content-analysis codes were source type plus 'amount of information', number of external sources, whether source credibility was addressed, 'balance' (takes a side = 1, balanced = 2) and 'facticity' (opinions = 1, mixed = 2, facts = 3); Table 3 splits the 120 accessed news sites into Public 15.00%, Established quality newspaper 60.83%, Established tabloid 2.5%, Not affiliated to a journalistic offline product 3.33%, Local 11.67%, Alternative news sites 6.67%
reason: quality instruments are not accuracy: the website coding measures presentation and source type (balance, facticity as opinion-vs-fact ratio, source transparency), never whether any claim on a visited page was false; the one categorical residue, 'Alternative News Sites', is an outlet type, not a truth judgement
notes: Confirms the abstract stage's UNSURE as an exclude. Two further reasons it could not serve as AUDIENCE EXPOSURE even if the coding qualified: the browsing is lab-task-constrained (45 economics students, five assigned CORA tasks, several tasks supplying the start page, so 112 of the 412 visits are the task's own pages), and the denominator is website visits within an assessment, not naturalistic consumption. HUMAN NOTE: 8/120 (6.67%) of accessed news sites were 'Alternative News Sites' and the paper states that sites 'that disseminate rather unreliable news were used little or not at all' without quantifying that claim. Sample stated as 50 students in the abstract but 45 in the Sample section.

title: 5G Awareness and its Link to COVID-19: Case of Zambians with Access to Internet
denominator: 258 online survey respondents (Zambia, June-July 2020)
evidence: Table 1, row 'Have you ever heard that symptoms of COVID-19 seem to be connected to 5G mobile network radiation?': Yes 162 (62.9%), No 72 (27.8%), Not sure 24 (9.3%), Total 258
reason: self-reported share who had ever heard a specific false claim
notes: REACH-flavoured but self-reported, so RECALL under the denominator rule (a share of people, from a questionnaire). The abstract rounds this to 'about 62%' and the body text to '63%'; Table 1's 62.9% is the exact figure. Belief in the claim is a separate item and out of scope (14.3% yes, 47.3% no, 38.4% not sure). Sampling is a WhatsApp-distributed online convenience questionnaire of internet-using Zambians, not a population sample, despite the Cochran calculation reported (95% CL, 5.4% margin, minimum 249).

title: BELIEVABILITY OF SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS: A STUDY OF ALLEGED FORCEFUL INJECTION OF MONKEY POX VIRUS IN SCHOOL CHILDREN
denominator: 332 Anambra State civil servants (of 341 distributed; 97.4% response)
evidence: Table 7 'Respondents' Exposure to the Army Deadly Vaccine Report': Yes 332 (100.0), No 0 (0.0); 'Thus, there was 100% exposure to the report, meaning that each of the respondents must have in one way or the other read or heard about the report'
reason: self-reported share exposed to a specific false claim (the October 2017 Nigerian army monkeypox 'deadly vaccine' rumour)
notes: HUMAN CHECK: a 100.0% exposure rate with zero non-exposed is not credible on its face and most likely reflects a leading or screening item; the questionnaire wording is not reproduced. The more usable figures are Table 8, exposed VIA SOCIAL MEDIA 284/332 (85.5%), Table 9, first-received platform (WhatsApp 65.7%, Facebook 16.9%, other 3.0%, no answer 14.5%), and Table 10, social media as the FIRST source 246/332 (74.1%). The believability items (Tables 11-17) measure belief, not exposure, and are out of scope. Data-quality flag: Figure 1's gender split is given as 50.9% male and 41.1% female, which sums to 92%.

title: User perceptions of fake news sharing behavior on social media through social networking sites
evidence: Text file contains 'Business Transformation Project's Holistic Agile Management' (Trad & Kalpic), The Business and Management Review 13(1), pp.102-119; the target article is absent
reason: cannot rule: the full text on disk is the wrong article from the same journal issue
notes: WRONG PDF. Nothing about fake news anywhere in the 60KB file. Needs a re-fetch of the correct article before it can be screened.

title: “The mask is not for you”: A framing analysis of pro- and anti-mask sentiment on Twitter
evidence: Extracted text is 4 KB of running heads plus three mangled table grids; no methods, results or sample-size prose survives
reason: cannot rule: extraction yielded table fragments only, denominators not reconstructable
notes: Visible fragments: an evidence-source table totalling 134 anti-mask and 440 pro-mask tweets, and a frame table where anti-mask frames include 'COVID-19 is a Hoax' (27) and 'Masks don't work' (21). Those two frames are the only falsity-adjacent categories; everything else is pro/anti stance, which the stance rule excludes. If the correct denominator is all coded tweets (574) then ~8% carry a false-claim frame, but the column-to-row alignment in the extracted grid is not trustworthy and the paper's own totals cannot be checked. Re-extract before using; leaning EXCLUDE on 'stance is not falsity' if the framing coding is confirmed to have no truth judgement.

title: Evaluation of Covid-19 Vaccine Sentiment on TikTok from 2020 to 2022
evidence: “Anti-vaccine was defined as any video that mocked vaccination, criticized the nature of COVID-19 vaccines, provided misinformation, or contained any material that would discourage people from getting a COVID vaccine.”
reason: stance is not falsity: the anti/pro coding is a discouragement/encouragement judgement, not a truth judgement, and misinformation is only one disjunct inside it
notes: Headline result is 109 anti- and 175 pro-vaccine videos out of 284 coded (342 viewed, 58 dropped as unrelated), i.e. 38.4% anti-vaccine. Sampling was by four hashtag sets sorted by 'most liked', so it is not a misinformation-only corpus, but the coding cannot be separated into a truth judgement. The 27% / 1% / 17% misinformation shares in the paper's Table 2 belong to Southwick, Ostrovsky & Chen, and Baumel, not to this study.

title: Auditing Google's Search Headlines as a Potential Gateway to Misleading Content
evidence: “we developed the coding scheme around a central ‘Stance’ category, which was used to categorize headlines based on their potential impact on search engine users' trust in the election's legitimacy”; codes are Sows Doubt / Imparts Trust / Provides Information
reason: stance is not falsity: headlines are coded by their potential effect on trust in the election, never by whether the headline is true
notes: OVERTURNS the abstract-stage INCLUDE. The authors state the falsity coding was NOT done and is future work: “Further investment in post hoc coding may also enable differentiation between types of potentially undermining content, such as misleading content and outright false content.” Their own example of a Sows Doubt headline, “Allegheny County ballot contractor accused of sending out late ballots in other counties”, is a true news report. 2,438 unique headlines coded out of a 5,600 stratified sample; the only shares of headlines promoting distrust appear in Figures 3, 4, 6 and 8 and are figure-only, with no percentage in the text. Media bias came from Ad Fontes; the paper reports NO effect of the Ad Fontes reliability score, so there is no credibility-list result either.

title: Impact of COVID-19 on HIV Prevention Access: A Multi-platform Social Media Infodemiology Study
denominator: 101 community-level signal posts (of 317 signal posts total; from 267,689 collected)
evidence: Table 1, code C-6 “PrEP used as a prevention method for COVID-19”: 43 posts, 42.57% of community-level signals; text: “similar incorrect conversations that PrEP could be used as a prevention method or precaution against COVID-19 infection (42.57%, n = 43)”
reason: a share of coded posts judged to carry a false claim, with a stated denominator
notes: OTHER SHARES: code B-9 “Users think they immune to COVID because they are on PrEP”, 14 posts = 12.07% of the 116 patient-level signals. Across the whole signal set the two misinformation codes are 43/317 = 13.6% and 14/317 = 4.4%; the paper never prints those. FOR A HUMAN: (1) the percentages the paper prints are shares of a coding LEVEL (provider / patient / community), not of the full post sample, so the extractor must choose the denominator deliberately; (2) the C-6 and B-9 example quotes are both users MOCKING or reporting the false belief rather than asserting it, so these codes mix assertion with commentary and probably overstate misinformation content; (3) the 317 signal posts were hand-selected from 11,222 COVID-filtered posts via topic modelling plus manual annotation, so the sampling denominator is not a random sample of PrEP talk. The paper is explicitly exploratory and its own limitations section warns the findings are not generalisable.

title: Generation Z: Media Consumption and MIL
denominator: 115 Greek respondents aged 12-24
evidence: “With regard to the question of the participants' being deceived by news that has later proven to be fake, 58,3% (n=67) responded positively”
reason: belief-conditional recall, eligible under ADDENDUM A: the item is anchored to news the respondent met and later learned was false
notes: Confirms the abstract-stage UNSURE/RECALL guess. Related item, frequency of encountering fake news: 28.7% not very often, 25.2% often, 22.6% rarely (sums to only 76.5%; the remaining categories exist only in Figure 11, which is figure-only, so a 'met fake news at least sometimes' share cannot be reconstructed from the text). CAVEATS for a human: N = 115 only, snowball recruitment through nation-wide social media groups plus pass-along to under-13s, ages 12-24, north Greece (Thrace and South Macedonia); no probability sampling and no weighting. Follow-up among the 67 deceived: 67.1% ignored the false news, 20.7% reported it, 12.2% commented.

title: Desórdenes informativos y polarización afectiva: emociones en publicaciones con desinformación en tres conflictos políticos brasileños en Twitter
denominator: 300 tweets (the 100 most-retweeted tweets from each of three Brazilian conflicts)
evidence: “se constata que cuando se observan los tres conflictos juntos, casi un tercio de las publicaciones de la muestra presentan algún tipo de trastorno de la información (95 en total)” [when the three conflicts are viewed together, almost a third of the sample's posts show some type of information disorder (95 in total)]; Tabla 4
reason: a share of coded posts judged false or misleading, with a stated denominator; veracity was checked against news sources, so it is an accuracy coding rather than a stance coding
notes: Tabla 4 breakdown (double-coded, so types sum to 118 over 95 tweets): misleading content 63, false connection 18, satire/parody 17, fabricated content 15, imposter 2, manipulated 2, false context 1; 140 tweets with no mis/disinformation; 65 tweets unavailable (deleted post or suspended account). FOR A HUMAN: the denominator is ambiguous. 95/300 = 31.7% is what the paper claims, but 65 of the 300 could not be coded, so the share among CODED tweets is 95/235 = 40.4%; the paper never says which it means. Second caveat: 17 of the 95 are “satire or parody”, which the review would not normally count as falsity, and the authors describe much of the “misleading content” category as users stating opinion as if it were truth. Excluding satire gives 78/300 = 26.0%. Per-conflict: CPI 40/100, abortion (100 minus 33 clean minus 37 unavailable) = 30/100, racism 25/100. Sample is the top-retweeted tweets by keyword, not a misinformation-selected corpus.

title: Spreading Fake Content via Social Media among Tertiary Level Students in Rangpur, Bangladesh
evidence: Table 3: “Spreading Fake Content via Social Media — Yes 111 (91.7%)”, i.e. respondents who think false information is disseminated via social media; Table 4 covers awareness of fake content, self-rated ability to identify it, and knowledge of verification tools
reason: concern and skills are not exposure: every item is a belief that fake content exists on social media, an attribution of blame to a platform, a motive, or a self-rated detection skill; none asks what the respondent encountered or how much of what they see is false
notes: OVERTURNS the abstract-stage INCLUDE. The 91.7% item is an existence belief (does fake content spread on social media, yes/no), not a claim about how much of the encountered content is false, so ADDENDUM B does not rescue it. BORDERLINE a human should look at: Table 3 “Types of Fake Content Notice More to the Social Media” gives political 64.5%, religious 50.4%, education 30.6%, job 30.6%, fun/entertainment 28.9%, economic 24%, communal 17.4%, sports 8.3% of the 121 respondents. Read as “which types do you notice MORE”, this is a salience ranking, not an encounter rate, and that is how I read it; read as “have you noticed fake political content”, 64.5% of 121 would be a RECALL estimate. The item stem is never printed. QUALITY WARNING: the abstract contradicts the tables repeatedly. Abstract says 92.7% believe fake content spreads (table: 91.7%), Facebook is the most popular platform at 71.9% (table: 99.2%; 71.9% is the awareness-of-fake-content figure), and 50.4% do not know the identification tools (table: 87.6%). Ages in Table 1 are given as 18-20 / 21-23 / 23-25, overlapping. N = 121 drawn from 8,000 students, described as simple random sampling but with no frame given. I would not extract from this paper without the questionnaire.

title: Assessment of the Quality and Reliability of Content Available on YouTube About Palpitations
evidence: “The Global Quality Score (GQS) and modified DISCERN score were used to analyze the quality and reliability of the information provided”; Table 2 reports presence of content types (symptoms 80.28%, cause/etiology 81.69%, treatment 59.15%)
reason: quality instruments are not accuracy (GQS, modified DISCERN) and coverage is not accuracy (Table 2 records whether a topic was MENTIONED, not whether it was right)
notes: OVERTURNS the abstract-stage INCLUDE. No video was ever coded true or false; no misinformation share exists anywhere in the paper. Watch the abstract's wording: it says “81.69% accurately described the etiological factors”, but the Table 2 row is “Information about cause/etiology?”, a presence check, and the instruments used cannot support the word 'accurately'. QUALITY WARNING, internal contradictions: Discussion says “64% were uploaded over a year ago” while Table 1 says 90.14%; Discussion says hospitals and doctors uploaded 42% while Table 1 gives 32.39% + 26.76% = 59.15%; Table 3 lists 'Patients suffering from the disease (n=16)' while Table 1 gives 3, and the columns sum to 84 against 71 videos. 71 videos, seven raters each judging their own keyword, no double coding and no reliability statistic.

title: Users' experience with health-related content on YouTube: an exploratory study
evidence: Fig. 8/Fig. 9: “41.6%, 28.8%, and 14.1% of the survey participants found HRC on YouTube useful, somewhat useful, or very useful”; “35.9% of the respondents perceived health-related content on YouTube as somewhat biased, while 31.1% considered it neutral. Only 12.6% ... believed that the content is biased”
reason: concern and skills are not exposure, and stance is not falsity: the survey measures perceived usefulness and perceived BIAS of health videos, never whether respondents met false content or how much of what they saw was false
notes: OVERTURNS the abstract-stage INCLUDE. N = 3,000 Prolific users, 33 countries, a well-run survey, but the outcome is the wrong construct: no item asks about encountering misinformation. Perceived bias is not perceived falsity, so ADDENDUM B does not apply. FIGURE-ONLY ITEM a human may want to check: Table 3 maps the bottom of the usefulness scale (1.0-1.80) to “Poor or misleading”, and Fig. 8 shows the full distribution of usefulness ratings; the text prints only the three positive bands (41.6 + 28.8 + 14.1 = 84.5%), so the ~15% rating videos 'not useful' or 'poor or misleading' exists only in the figure. Even if read off the figure, that is a usefulness rating, not a falsity judgement. Related: 2.6% (n=79) of the 3,000 said they avoid health content on YouTube because of quality concerns.

title: “No claims, no trials, no compensation. Just roll up your sleeve”: social media communication on vaccine uptake sentiments in Canada
evidence: Table 1: “Misinformation and conspiracy beliefs 96% (BC before) / 97% (ON before) / 76% (BC after) / 81% (ON after)”, footnote “*Percentage shows the topic occurrence from the total Tweets within the frame”
reason: stance is not falsity: these are LDA topic-occurrence weights for a sentiment FRAME, not a per-tweet truth judgement, and the frame explicitly contains tweets that debunk misinformation as well as tweets carrying it
notes: OVERTURNS the abstract-stage INCLUDE. Two reasons. (1) The category is talk ABOUT misinformation. The authors say so: “two types of vaccine-related health mavenism: misinformation circulation from the public and retweeting by subject experts and government officials demystifying with scientific evidence”, and “the myths were also busted with scientific evidence by some tweeters”. Table 2's own example tweets include “It is up to people on social media NOT to share disinformation & misinformation about vaccines” and a debunking by a PhD microbiologist. A 96% figure is not a claim that 96% of tweets were false. (2) The denominator is self-referential and undefined: “topic occurrence from the total Tweets within the frame”. 20,000 tweets were analysed (5,000 before and 5,000 after in each of BC and ON, drawn sequentially rather than randomly from 67,923 BC and 214,768 ON geotagged tweets), neutral-sentiment tweets were dropped before topic modelling, and the frame denominators are never given. QUALITY WARNING: the abstract says antivaccine expressions fell “9% and 6% in BC and ON”, but the Results text says ON “dropped by 18%” and Table 1 shows ON 91% to 73%. VADER is stated to be insensitive to sarcasm, which matters a great deal for a misinformation category.

title: Like-minded sources on Facebook are prevalent but not polarizing
denominator: all Facebook Feed content exposures of the control-group participants (23,377 US adult participants randomised; control group roughly half), 24 Sept to 23 Dec 2020
evidence: “the average proportion of exposures decreased ... from 0.76% to 0.55% for content from misinformation repeat offenders (a reduction of 0.62 views per day on average)”; misinformation repeat offenders are “sources identified by Facebook as repeatedly posting misinformation”
reason: a share of what people actually saw, measured from platform logs, attributable to sources flagged for repeatedly posting misinformation
notes: Confirms the abstract-stage UNSURE/EXPOSURE guess, and specifically on the untrustworthy-source share rather than the headline like-minded measure. The like-minded / cross-cutting numbers (50.4% vs 14.7% for the median user; 53.7% control-group exposure) are ideological alignment and are EXCLUDED by ADDENDUM D; the repeat-offender list is a falsity-based designation (Facebook's fact-checker-driven repeat-offender status), so it qualifies. OTHER VALUES: treatment group 0.55%; comparison quantities of the same shape are uncivil content 3.15% (control) and 2.81% (treatment), and slur-word content 0.034% / 0.030%. Context shares: civic content is a median 6.9% and news a median 6.7% of what users see, so 0.76% of ALL exposures is a large fraction of the political slice. FOR A HUMAN: (1) 0.76% is a control-group mean during an experiment, not a population descriptive; the descriptive arm of the paper (231 million monthly Facebook users) reports like-minded exposure, not repeat-offender exposure, so the population-level equivalent is not in this paper. (2) The denominator is exposures, not users, so this is EXPOSURE and not REACH. (3) The measure is source-level, not item-level: content from a flagged source is counted whether or not the particular post is false. (4) Measurement details for the repeat-offender classifier are in Supplementary Information section 1.3, which is not in the file on disk. (5) Meta co-authored the paper and supplied the classifier.

title: Exploring social media strategies use during the presidential campaign of the 2023 general elections in Nigeria
evidence: Table 1: 'The spread of misinformation on social media significantly impacted the presidential campaign' AS 304 / A 42 / U 2 / SD 11 / D 6, Total 365, mean 4.5
reason: Concern is not exposure: the only quantitative items are Likert agreement with impact statements, not a claim about how much of what respondents met was false
notes: n=365 returned of 385. Every misinformation-related item is about the campaign's integrity or impact, not about the respondent's own encounters; addendum B test (does the statement claim HOW MUCH of the encountered content is false?) fails. Qualitative section is anecdotal quotes only. Figures 1-2 are images not in the text dump but their captions are response-rate and impact-of-limitations, not exposure.

title: Assess Nurses' Social Media Conduct's Effect on Patient Trust
evidence: Table 4 'Key Challenges in Accessing Health Information via Social Media', Misinformation: Great Extent 18.5% + Very Great Extent 25.6% = 44.1%; prose 'Misinformation was a notable concern for 44.1% of respondents'
reason: Concern is not exposure: 44.1% is a challenge/barrier severity rating on a 'least extent - very great extent' scale, not a share who encountered misinformation

title: Therapeutic frequencies in digital music culture: content analysis on technical accuracy
denominator: 150 digital music contents titled with a specific Hz value across 7 platforms
evidence: Table 2 "Distribution of the technical accuracy of the contents" (n=150): Containing the Promised Frequency 12 (8%); Containing Incorrect/Incomplete Frequency 138 (92%); text: "The fact that the promised Hertz value was found in only 12 contents (8%) points to a serious inconsistency"
reason: item-level factual verification of each item's own claim against FFT spectrum analysis, on a topic-conditional sample (Addendum C)
notes: Purposive criterion sample: content on YouTube, YouTube Music, Instagram, Spotify, Fizy, Apple Music, Deezer with at least 10,000 interactions and a specific Hz value (432/528/639 Hz) in the title or description. Each file's first stable 60 s was FFT-analysed three times; the item was counted accurate if the titled value was the dominant spectral peak within +/-3 Hz. Two-coder content analysis, Krippendorff alpha 0.82 (that alpha covers the discursive coding, not the FFT test, which is instrumental). FOR THE EXTRACTOR: the accuracy claim tested is narrow - whether the audio actually contains the frequency named in the title - and NOT whether the health claims (DNA repair, cellular resonance) are true; those are never coded. Second figure, 86% (129/150) containing only low-tempo music, is a musical-structure descriptive, not a falsity measure. Denominator is topic-conditional: every item in the sample makes a healing-frequency claim, so record the restriction.

The 75% is High + Very High combined; 10% report low or very low. title: From labels to influencers: evaluating the alignment of nitrate and beetroot juice claims on sports supplement marketing with scientific consensus

reason: no numeric value (rule F) - the disinformation-sharing measure is a five-item Likert composite reported only as a mean, with regression coefficients and R2 = 0.389; no share of respondents
notes: Confirms the abstract-stage doubt. Percentages in the paper are demographics only (Table 2). HUMAN FLAG: the abstract says "Based on the simulated findings", and the results read as a template - the data may not be real. Would be unsafe to extract from even if a share appeared.

title: PENGARUH PENGGUNAAN MEDIA SOSIAL BERMUATAN INTOLERAN TERHADAP SIKAP TOLERANSI MAHASISWA PPKn UNIVERSITAS TANJUNGPURA
evidence: Tabel 2 "Bentuk Paparan Konten Intoleran di Media Sosial" (percentage of students who had ever encountered each): hate speech 92%, content demeaning an ethnic group or culture 93%, negative stereotypes 80%, comments cornering a group 90%, discriminatory images 83%, hateful videos 85%, intolerant content packaged as humour 95%
reason: stance is not falsity - every one of the seven exposure rows codes hate, stereotype or discrimination, with no truth judgement anywhere
notes: The shape is right (percentage of the 100 students who had ever encountered each content type, so denominator and construct machinery are there) but no row is about false content. "Hoaks" appears in the abstract's narrative list of intolerant content types and in the literature review, and never as a table row or a percentage - so there is no hoax-encounter share to take. Table 3 reports tolerance attitudes, not exposure. English translation of the Tabel 2 header: "Forms of exposure to intolerant content on social media / Percentage of students who had ever encountered it".

title: More than meets the eye
evidence: EMBO reports science & society feature on scientific data visualization; no misinformation measure anywhere in the text
reason: review/commentary; not an empirical study and no falsity coding
notes: Text confirmed to be the right article (Rinaldi, EMBO reports 13(10):895-899, doi 10.1038/embor.2012.135). It is a magazine feature on scientific visualization; the abstract stage flagged it only because the title is uninformative.

title: Social Media Outrage in Response to a School-Based Substance Use Survey: Qualitative Analysis
evidence: Table 2: 'Conspiratorial or irrational 19 (14.3)' of N=133 negative comments; and 'Although there was no overarching code for misinformation, comments in each of these categories ... logically presupposed inaccurate information'
reason: no falsity coding (Rule G) — the category is a thinking-style disjunction, not an item-level truth judgement
notes: The 14.3% category is defined as 'comments displaying conspiratorial thinking or creation of implications that demonstrably surpass a reasonable person standard' (mostly Nazi-Germany comparisons), i.e. rhetoric, not verified false claims; its denominator is also the negative subset (133) not the full 207. The 99/207 (47.8%) aggregate lumps parental autonomy/privacy, child protective services, conspiratorial-or-irrational, prevent-abuse and hiding-something, and the authors state explicitly there was no misinformation code; 7.2% (15/207) is the share that DID contain factual information, an inverse-coverage measure, not a falsity share.

title: A Transparent Digital Election Campaign? The Insights and Significance of Political Advertising Archives for Debates on Electoral Regulation
evidence: Results report ad spend and archive coverage only, e.g. '£2,814,066 was spent on online adverts. This constitutes 14% of the total possible spend'; the only occurrences of 'false' are 'false positives' in the actor-matching procedure
reason: no falsity coding — ads are coded for advertiser type and spend, never for accuracy
notes: Facebook and Google ad-archive transparency study (UK 2019 general election). 'Disinformation' appears once, in a cited DCMS committee report title. Nothing to extract.

title: Using Social Listening for Digital Public Health Surveillance of Human Papillomavirus Vaccine Misinformation Online: Exploratory Study
evidence: Results section is Table 1, a qualitative CDC-attribute feasibility matrix ('Social listening opportunities' / 'Social listening limitations'); no post counts, no denominator, no percentage anywhere
reason: reports no data — feasibility assessment with no observations (Rule J)
notes: A 'misinformation' sentiment category was built into the Brandwatch dashboard but no volume or share of posts in it is ever reported. The only numbers in the paper are a price (>=US $2500 annually) and dates. Authors also state the AI classification 'was not completely accurate upon periodic spot reviews'.

title: Descaling psoriasis narratives on TikTok: A cross-sectional study
denominator: 47 educational psoriasis TikTok videos (of 134 English-language #Psoriasis videos screened from the first 200)
evidence: "We found that of the 47 educational videos, around 55% (n = 26) were classed as reliable whilst the remaining 45% (n = 21) were deemed unreliable."
reason: qualifying content share: videos judged unreliable against NICE guidelines/CKS
notes: Denominator is topic/type-conditional (educational videos only), acceptable under Addendum rule C; record the restriction. 21/47 = 44.7%, printed as 'around 45%'. Sample construction: first 200 #Psoriasis videos, 65 dropped as non-English and 1 off-topic, leaving 134; only the 47 educational ones were reliability-coded, so the whole-sample equivalent would be 21/134 = 15.7% (NOT printed by the paper — do not report it as theirs). Table 1 breaks the 47 down by creator (Dermatologist 16 reliable / 0 unreliable; health-wellness guru 2 / 13; other 8 / 8) but the row totals give 47 only if read as 16+0+2+13+8+8 = 47, consistent. Unreliable content described as advising discontinuation of prescribed medication, i.e. advice contrary to a standard, so accuracy not merely quality. Engagement figures (2 million likes reliable vs 850,000 unreliable) are totals, not a share, and Figure 2 (proportion of likes by source) is figure-only. Single-author research letter, two pages, no reported intercoder reliability.

title: #mediterraneandiet: A Content Analysis of Mediterranean Diet - Related Information on TikTok
evidence: "Preliminary results suggest two main interpretations of the MD on TikTok"; the only quantitative statement in the whole item is the intercoder reliability, 'k = .84'
reason: no numeric value (Rule F) — one-page conference abstract with no accuracy share
notes: 200 TikTok videos coded on 62 variables, but the abstract reports no falsity or misleading-content variable and no percentage. Findings are stated qualitatively ('clear examples emerged of individuals conflating these two concepts'); 'potentially-misleading online content' appears only in the conclusion as a generic worry. Current Developments in Nutrition supplement abstract (2 KB).

title: The Impact of COVID-19 on Conspiracy Hypotheses and Risk Perception in Italy: Infodemiological Survey Study Using Google Trends
evidence: "Through the iterative comparison of RSVs, it was possible to estimate that, in the last 12 months, this query represented about 0.04% of COVID-19-related web searches."
reason: not exposure — Google Trends relative search volume measures search interest (what users asked for), not misinformation content encountered
notes: BOUNDARY CALL, flagged for a human. The 0.04% is the only share-shaped number in the paper and it does have a denominator (COVID-19-related web searches), but (i) the unit is a search query about the engineered-virus claim, not a piece of content the user met, which the 'what was MET is what counts' rule puts outside RECALL/EXPOSURE, and (ii) Google Trends returns only normalised relative search volumes, so the 0.04% is inferred by chained RSV comparisons, not observed; there is no counted denominator. Everything else in the paper is RSV percentage changes and t tests. The heat-map index (Figures 4, 6) is a within-pair split of conspiracy vs antihoax queries, again relative and figure-only.

title: Misinformation versus Facts: Understanding the Influence of News regarding COVID-19 Vaccines on Vaccine Uptake
denominator: ~4,000,000 geotagged US English vaccine-related tweets and retweets, 19 Apr-30 Jun 2021
evidence: "we detected 26,998 fake-news-related (fake news, conspiracy theories, unreliable contents, or extremely biased news) and 456,061 fact-related tweets"; sample described as "Nearly four million geotagged tweets as well as the retweets ... were collected. The average number of geotagged tweets per state is 79,894"
reason: qualifying source-level share of tweets linking to unreliable domains
notes: SOURCE-LEVEL (Addendum rule H): classification is by URL domain against a Columbia Journalism Review list of 1,125 domains merging PolitiFact, FactCheck, OpenSources and Snopes lists; no tweet was itself truth-coded. THREE THINGS FOR A HUMAN. (1) The percentage is NOT printed; 0.68% is 26,998 divided by the stated 'nearly four million', and the exact corpus N never appears (79,894 x 51 gives ~4.07M). Extraction must decide whether an approximate denominator is acceptable. (2) The flagged group is a disjunction: 'fake news, conspiracy theories, unreliable contents, or extremely biased news', and the paper defines the last branch as sources that 'come from a particular point of view and may rely on propaganda, decontextualized information, and opinions distorted as facts' — i.e. it mixes a credibility list with a hyperpartisan one, which Addendum rule D treats as different things. (3) Construct could equally be OBSERVED SHARING: the units are tweets including retweets and quotes carrying a link, from platform data. Also available: 456,061 fact-related tweets (11.4%); 10,925 unique fake-news users vs 159,283 fact users, with no total-user denominator printed; 6,839 users in both groups, '62.6% and 4.3% of the fake-news-related users and fact-related users' (an overlap share within the flagged group, not a prevalence); state-level user percentages exist only in Figures 1(a) and 1(b).

title: Hesitancy towards COVID-19 vaccines on social media in Canada
evidence: "Notable too was the extent of misinformation and misrepresentation in user comments." — the only table in the paper (Table 1) lists the 19 source articles and their comment counts; no code frequencies are reported
reason: no numeric value (Rule F) — qualitative thematic analysis, no share of the 1145 comments is given for any code
notes: 1145 CBC comments from 19 articles, coded inductively into themes with illustrative quotes only. The paper's contribution is conceptual (distinguishing 'misrepresentation' from misinformation); it never counts either. The percentages that do appear (80% of Canadians vaccinated, 11% unvaccinated, 20% in a cited survey) are national statistics and one article headline, not properties of the comment sample.

title: How Official Social Media Affected the Infodemic among Adults during the First Wave of COVID-19 in China
evidence: The infodemic scale's five items: "the information I received exceeded my capacity to cope with it"; "I felt panicky when I saw the amount of information"; "I constantly sought information"; "I often forgot to respond to other important messages"; "I found it difficult to obtain reliable information when I needed help" (5-point agree scale, used only as a latent variable)
reason: concern and overload are not exposure — the 'infodemic' construct measures information overload and difficulty finding reliable information, not misinformation encountered
notes: 1398 WeChat respondents. No share of any kind is reported for the infodemic construct: results are PLS-SEM path coefficients (IQ to infodemic beta = -0.294; cascades 0.242; support -0.387) plus mediation and moderation tests. The only percentages in the paper are the demographic composition table. Even if a share had been printed, no item asks about encountering false or misleading content.

title: Followers do not dictate the virality of news outlets on social media
evidence: "According to NewsGuard ratings, our dataset comprises 898 reliable sources and 131 nonreliable ones. We performed a sampling of 131 reliable sources to have two comparable samples."
reason: no qualifying share — outcomes are engagement and follower growth-rate distributions by reliability label; no share of posts, engagement or users is reported
notes: 57M Facebook posts, 2008-2022, from 1000+ NewsGuard-rated outlets in four languages via CrowdTangle. The reliability comparison is Mann-Whitney tests on growth-rate distributions between 131 Questionable and 131 distance-matched Reliable pages, plus fitted Laplace/Burr parameters — no prevalence. The only share-shaped number is 131/1029 = 12.7% of outlets rated non-reliable, which is a property of the NewsGuard sampling frame (outlets NewsGuard rated AND that have a Facebook page), not a prevalence in any audience or content population; the paper never computes it. Flagged in case a human wants it as source-list composition.

title: The COVID-19 infodemic as a major driver for vaccine hesitancy in conflict settings: a mixed-method study
evidence: Table 3: "The COVID-19 vaccine infodemic's effect on health decisions — No 220 (55.00), Yes 152 (38.00), No answers 28 (07.00)"; Table 2 the same shape for effect on physical and mental health (Yes 134, 33.50)
reason: perceived impact is not exposure — the item asks whether misinformation AFFECTED the respondent, so a respondent who encountered it but was unaffected is not in the numerator (the logic of Addendum rule E)
notes: Overturns the first-pass INCLUDE, which was presumably taken on the abstract's 38%. Neither survey item asks about encountering misinformation; both ask about its effect on the respondent, and the paper's own prose reads the majority answer as respondents who 'think vaccine misinformation has no negative impact on their health'. Non-response is 6-7% on both items, so the denominator for the 38% is all 400 surveyed, not the 372 who answered. Table 4's hesitancy reasons ('Many rumors about the vaccine' 55, 13.75%) are reasons for refusal, are multiple-response, and are percentaged over 400 although the question was asked only of the 243 who said they would not take the vaccine — the eight reason rows sum to 261 responses, so that denominator is wrong as printed; not extractable either way. The social-listening arm (1869 documents: 1855 tweets, 14 Facebook posts, Jan-Apr 2022) mentions '41 categories of COVID-19-related narratives, including ... misinformation, disinformation' but reports no counts per category — only six themes with quotes. Prose also says 'nearly half of the participants (N = 243, 61%)', which is not nearly half.

title: Assessing the Quality and Safety of Do-It-Yourself Cosmetic Neuromodulator Injection Tutorials on YouTube
evidence: Table 1 'Summary of guideline adherence across assessed videos': Reconstitution and dilution process 7.5%; Understanding of neuromuscular and structural anatomy 66%; Proper dose determination 17%; ... 'Videos covered an average of 1.51 (SD = 1.22) out of the seven guidelines.'
reason: coverage is not accuracy: the 40 videos are scored on whether they COVER each of seven Medication Guide Insert points, plus credentials and engagement; no item is judged true or false
notes: Two-page Letter. Denominator is 40 of 101 screened videos. Nearest thing to an accuracy figure is a practice measure, not a truth judgement: 82% used sterile technique (so 18% did not) and 4.7% demonstrated sharps disposal; the paper frames all seven as guideline COVERAGE ('videos covered an average of 1.51 out of the seven guidelines'), and 39% 'lacked a discussion of complications' is explicitly an omission. Flagged as the borderline in this batch under addendum rule on 'demonstrates a practice contrary to a standard'.

title: Vaccination Conversations on X in Spanish and Catalan: Qualitative Content Analysis
evidence: Table 2 'Descriptive overview of theme frequency': Theme 2 vaccine skepticism and criticism 93 (24.2%) of 384 tweets; theme 2 text: 'Some posts reflected doubts or criticisms about the efficacy, safety, or necessity of vaccines.'
reason: no falsity coding (rule G): the only counted category is a stance/skepticism THEME that mixes doubt, criticism and complaint with false claims, and stance is not falsity
notes: Misinformation is the FIFTH SUBTHEME of theme 2 and carries no count anywhere in the paper - only illustrative quotes in Table 3. The theme is a disjunction ('doubts or criticisms about the efficacy, safety, or necessity'), so an item in it need not be false. Theme 3 (provaccination, 18.7%) explicitly contains a 'debunking myths' subtheme, confirming the code frame is stance-based. Sample: 384 tweets subsampled from 479,734; NodeXL random sample of unknown sampling frame, which the authors flag as a limitation.

title: Perception of Information and Disinformation on Social Media
evidence: Figure 1 / Results: Proposition 3 'The greatest spread of rumours and disinformation on the internet occurs via social media' - 67.6% totally or mostly agree (34.0% + 33.6%), n = 1,800; Proposition 4 'Continuous exposure to information on social media helps distinguish fake from real news' - 43.1% mostly or totally agree
reason: concern/belief about the medium is not exposure (and skills are not exposure): neither of the two disinformation items asks how much of what the respondent SEES is false
notes: Well-powered survey, N = 1,800 Spanish 14-24 year olds, quota sampled, Oct-Nov 2024; all four propositions printed verbatim with full 5-point distributions. Rule B was the hard call here: proposition 3 is a comparative claim about WHICH channel spreads most disinformation, not a claim about the quantity of false content the respondent encounters, so it fails rule B's test; proposition 4 is a self-assessed detection ability item, explicitly out. Worth a human eye if the review ever widens to perceived-locus items.

title: Between truth and doubt: The credibility of social networks, an analysis of perceptions of truthfulness
evidence: 'users' credibility in social media, especially related to facebook showed that 42.3% express they believe in the information presented on this social media, notwithstanding the majority (57.7%) shared that they do not trust the information displayed there' (n = 456)
reason: concern/trust is not exposure: the only quantified item is generalised trust in Facebook content, which makes no claim about how much of what respondents see is false
notes: 5-question Google Forms survey of 456 in Bogota; the only other number is 249/456 (about 55%) naming Facebook as their main news gateway. Numbers appear in text and in Figures 2-4 only; no tables. Quality problems: the sample is described as 87% aged 18-25 and 13% aged 30-55 with no remainder; the survey instrument is never reproduced, so the exact wording behind 42.3%/57.7% is unknown; the article is padded with long passages of unsourced generalities. Would become an UNCERTAIN rather than an EXCLUDE only if the item turned out to ask about the share of false content, which the printed text does not support.

title: Use and Misuse of Social Media and National Security in Africa: A Delicate Balance between Order and Liberty in Kenya
evidence: Table 2 'Participation in Social Media Activism and Unknowingly Participating in Misinformation': Pearson r = .621, p = .000, N = 262. No frequency or percentage is reported for the misinformation variable anywhere in the paper.
reason: no numeric value (rule F applied to a construct that is otherwise right): the misinformation-participation variable is reported only as a correlation, never as a share
notes: The construct would have been self-reported sharing (RECALL) had a share been printed. Only percentages given are platform use (WhatsApp 81.6%, TikTok 58.0% ...), participation in or observation of activism (73.1%), most influential platform (X 52.1%) and perceived riskiest platform (X 59.4%) - all perceived risk, which the criteria exclude. Quality problem for a human: the announced sample is 384 users, but both correlation tables report N = 262, and the discrepancy is never explained; no descriptive table for any survey item.

title: Assessing Alopecia Areata Misinformation: Social Media Analysis
denominator: 98 YouTube videos retrieved under #alopecia / #alopeciatreatment, 17-24 July 2024
evidence: 'Of the YouTube videos analyzed, 76% (n=75) were categorized as "other," 13% (n=13) as "accurate and medical data-backed," and 10% (n=10) as "limited or anecdotal evidence"; no videos were classified as "misinformed and/or false."'
reason: explicit falsity category ('misinformed and/or false': inaccurate or misleading claims) applied item by item to a topic-defined sample, not a misinformation-only corpus
notes: Four further qualifying shares for extraction, all CONTENT PREVALENCE: TikTok 1% (n=2) of 222 videos misinformed/false; and two topic-conditional denominators in the sense of addendum C - among the 23 YouTube videos that actually addressed AA treatment, 0% misinformed/false, and among the 52 such TikTok videos, 3.8% (n=2, printed as 3%). Percentages in the abstract use the full platform denominator (222) while the Results section uses the treatment-only denominator (52), so 'limited or anecdotal evidence' appears as both 5% and 23% for the same n=12; the extractor must record which denominator each value uses. Quality: single reviewer coded everything, no interrater reliability, one-week collection window; a chi-square comparing platforms (P=.15) is run on 2 misinformed videos.

title: Untrustworthy sources on Facebook and Instagram in 2020: Concentrated exposure but no attitudinal effects
denominator: all content viewed in Feed by the median active US adult Facebook user, 7 Aug - 23 Sep 2020 (231 million monthly US accounts)
evidence: 'Overall, just 1.1 and 0.1% of the content that the median user saw on Facebook and Instagram, respectively, were from an untrustworthy source.'
reason: behavioural exposure share with a platform-population denominator
notes: SOURCE-LEVEL (addendum H): 'untrustworthy source' = a Page, group, domain or Instagram account that posted or shared two or more items rated false or altered media by IFCN fact-checkers, so the value is the share of exposure coming FROM flagged sources, not the share of exposures that were themselves false. Record it as source-level, not item-level. Further qualifying values for extraction. AUDIENCE EXPOSURE: Instagram median 0.1%; top 2.5% of FB users saw 14% or more from untrustworthy sources, top 2.5% of IG users 10% or more; among the top 2.5% of FB users, 60.9% or more of civic content seen from Pages and 57.1% or more from groups was from untrustworthy sources. CONCENTRATION: 23% of Facebook users and 11% of Instagram users (about 53 million and 22 million accounts) accounted for 80% of exposure; the top 20% of FB users accounted for 75.9% and the top 20% of IG users for 90.1% of total exposure to this content; within untrustworthy content, the top 0.5% of untrustworthy Pages (235 Pages) drew 74% of exposure to untrustworthy Page content, the top 0.5% of untrustworthy domains (13 domains) 70%, and the top 0.5% of untrustworthy groups (199 groups) 46%. Also: untrustworthy Pages were 52.8% of total untrustworthy-source exposure on Facebook, and only 0.4% of Pages followed by the median FB user were untrustworthy (a following measure, not exposure). The 2020 US Facebook and Instagram Election Study; preregistered (https://osf.io/dt6hz/); Meta co-authored but academics held analysis control. Several of the exposure percentiles cite supplementary tables S40/S41 which are not in this file, though the headline values are printed in the main text.

title: Quality Assessment of Videos about Radiotherapy-Related Oral Mucositis on YouTube in Brazil
denominator: 104 YouTube videos on radiotherapy-related oral mucositis (Brazil, from first 200 retrieved)
evidence: "Eleven videos (10.6%) were classified as 'poor' because they contained at least one incorrect information"; Table 2
reason: accuracy coding alongside the quality scale, so eligible on the accuracy part
notes: Table 2 gives per-variable shares of videos scoring 1-2 (information totally or partially wrong): head and neck cancer definition 7 (6.7%), mucositis definition 2 (1.9%), signs and symptoms 1 (1.0%), prevention/treatment 2 (1.9%), radiotherapy definition 0, frequency 0. The 32.7% 'fair' category is an OMISSION measure (information not mentioned) and is not accuracy. Denominator 104 after excluding 5 short, 39 long and 52 off-topic videos.

title: Understanding Sputnik News Agency internet traffic analysis
evidence: Text ends mid-Results at section 5.3 ("points of web access"); sections 5.4-5.9 answering unique visitors, bounce rate, traffic source, pages per visit and time on site are absent, as are the discussion and references
reason: full text truncated; the audience-size sections that could carry a source-level reach share are missing
notes: What IS present carries no qualifying share: Table 1 gives Alexa country RANKS (Romania 898, Moldova 52 in 2018), not shares; the country-of-access percentages (Russia 51.2%, Romania 8.7% in 2018) are a breakdown of Sputnik's own visitors, i.e. inside a single flagged-source corpus, not a prevalence. If the missing pages report Gemius real users as a share of the Moldovan online population that would be a source-level REACH figure (rule H) and the paper becomes eligible. Sputnik is designated a disinformation outlet by state attribution/EUvsDisinfo, not by a credibility rating service, which is itself a boundary a human may want to rule on.

title: How accurate are news mentions of scholarly output? A content analysis
evidence: "In total, 42.5% of the sample records have some kind of error, among which 27.1% have type A error... and 15.4% have type B error"; error taxonomy is dead links, inaccessible pages, false-positive mentions and metadata mismatches (title, author, journal, publication date)
reason: not a falsity judgement about content - the accuracy measured is bibliographic and link integrity of Altmetric database records, a bespoke data-quality checklist, not the truth of any claim
notes: Denominator 2,956 of 3,000 sampled news-mention records. The nearest candidate, "inaccurate news mention (7.9%)", is a record-level linkage/metadata error, not a misreport of a study's findings: the coding compares only title, author, journal and publication date. FLAG: the text is truncated at p.4080 of 4075-4096, so Table 3 with all 14 specific error types is not visible; if a human wants certainty, check Table 3 for any code that judges whether the news article misstates the research finding.

title: A web-based cross-sectional observational study on the analysis of information on diabetes on Instagram
denominator: 448 relevant Instagram posts (of 600 top-performing posts under six diabetes hashtags)
evidence: Table 8 Authenticity of information: True 208 (46.43%), False 19 (4.24%), Cannot be determined 221 (49.33%); "misinformation was reported in 19 posts (4.24%)"
reason: posts judged true/false against the latest WHO diabetes guidelines, an accuracy coding
notes: QUALITY PROBLEM the extractor must record: authenticity could NOT be determined for 221/448 posts (49.33%), so 4.24% is a lower bound over the full sample; among posts where a judgement was made the share false is 19/227 = 8.4%. The Discussion misdescribes this category - "as much as 49.33% of the published posts originated from unverifiable sources" - conflating undetermined authenticity with source verification; Table 4 shows the unverified-SOURCE share is 39.29%. Other sloppiness in the paper: Table 2 prints images as 424 (94.64%) in the abstract but 96.64% in the results, and a garbled "810.71%" for memes. The coverage figures in Table 7 (92.19% no prevalence information, etc.) are OMISSION measures, not accuracy.

title: Navigating the digital frontier: protecting adolescents in the age of mobile internet
evidence: Header on p.402 reads "COMMENT"; the piece has no methods, no sample and no results, only policy description: "the spread of cyberbullying, misinformation, and harmful content increases psychological stress"
reason: review/commentary - no data collected, so no share of anything can be reported
notes: Confirms the abstract stage's UNSURE. The two figures it does print are borrowed from other sources and are not misinformation measures: 202.02 million Chinese adolescent internet users (CNNIC 2024) and a 52.7% myopia rate (Xinhua). Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 are a time trend of user counts and a map of national policies.

title: Public responses to COVID-19 information from the public health office on Twitter and YouTube: implications for research practice
evidence: Tables 1-2 report log-likelihood keyness of key phrases only; 'Conspiracy and misinformation are not, upon a closer read, the main focus of key Twitter content'
reason: no falsity coding - corpus-linguistic keyness plus qualitative themes; no share of tweets or comments individually judged false
notes: Restored pages add the full keyness tables, qualitative reading and discussion, and confirm the truncated ruling. The paper does report concentration figures ('Approximately 61% of comments were posted by 10% of users, and about 20% of comments were posted by 1% of users'; '25% of tweets were posted by 10% of users, and about 7.5% of tweets by 1% of users') but these are concentration of ALL engagement on CPHO posts, not of misinformation exposure or sharing, so they do not meet the CONCENTRATION construct. Ruling UNCHANGED from previous EXCLUDE.

title: Covid-19 Information Behaviour of Social Media Users in Nigeria
evidence: Table 3 'Challenges encountered by social media users in Nigeria when seeking for Covid-19 information on social media', row 'Fake news/misinformation': 204 (58.6) strongly agree, 118 (33.9) agree; prose: 'table 3 shows that 204 (58.6%) of the respondents strongly agreed that fake news/misinformation constitutes a challenge'
reason: general concern item (Addendum B): agreement that misinformation 'constitutes a challenge' says nothing about whether or how much was encountered
notes: RULING CHANGED from UNCERTAIN to EXCLUDE. The restored pages contain the missing Table 3 AND the item wording, which the truncated file lacked. The wording is the excluded form named verbatim in Addendum B ('misinformation is a threat, a problem, a challenge'), so the rule E fallback no longer applies. Denominator would have been 348 respondents; combined agree+strongly agree = 92.5%. FOR A HUMAN: the table CAPTION says 'challenges ENCOUNTERED ... when seeking Covid-19 information', which pulls toward an encounter reading, while the item text is a problem-agreement item. I ruled on the item text. If the project decides the caption governs, this becomes an INCLUDE at 92.5% (or 58.6% top box) of 348, RECALL.

title: A Quality Assessment of Information Available on Renal Cancer on YouTube
denominator: 120 YouTube videos returned for 'renal cancer' meeting inclusion criteria
evidence: 'Misinformation was found in 49.7% of the videos analysed, and 22.5% contained moderate to high levels of misinformation. The other 50.3% were scored as having no misinformation.' (Results, alongside Table 4 'Quality and misinformation analysis')
reason: misinformation coded on a 5-point Likert accuracy tool against EAU/AUA guidelines, share of a general video sample
notes: Ruling UNCHANGED from previous INCLUDE, but the restored pages supply the value, which the truncated file did not. INTERNAL CONTRADICTION the extractor must resolve: Results say 49.7% with misinformation / 50.3% none, whereas the Discussion says 49.2% ('proportion of videos with misinformation (49.2%)') and Table 4 gives misinformation score 1 = 61 (50.8%), which implies 49.2%. 49.2% is the arithmetically consistent figure; 49.7% is what the paper leads with. Secondary share: 22.5% at moderate-to-high misinformation (scores 3-5). The paper also runs modified DISCERN and GQS; per the quality-instrument rule those are NOT eligible - only the misinformation Likert is.

title: A Tumblr thematic analysis of perinatal health: Where users go to seek support
denominator: 235 Tumblr text posts on perinatal health collected over 4 days
evidence: 'Misinformation, although present on the platform, accounted for only 3% of the total sample of posts (7/235).' Supported by section 4.1.6: 'Of the 30 posts, 7 were flagged as "misinformation" due to the content of the post.'
reason: 7 posts individually flagged false on content (non-evidence-based treatments and natural remedies) over a general 235-post sample
notes: RULING CHANGED from EXCLUDE to INCLUDE. The truncated file showed only the mixed theme label 'Misinformation/advertisement' (n = 30), which correctly triggered rule G / the rule I disjunction. The restored pages DISAGGREGATE that category: of the 30, 7 were individually flagged as misinformation on content, 7 were podcast/book/documentary ads and 16 were doctor ads, and the paper computes 7/235 = 3% over the whole sample. So the disjunction defect does not touch the 3% figure. CAVEATS: falsity judgement is by two co-authors with no reported reliability statistic, and the flagged examples are promotional posts pushing natural remedies, so the misinformation/advertising boundary is thin. Denominator is small and the window is only 4 days.

title: Social Media as a Learning Tool: Impacts on Collaborative Learning and Knowledge Sharing
